title: Dynamics
intro: How quantum states change in time: the Schrödinger equation and its solution $e^{-iHt}$, the Schrödinger and Heisenberg pictures, wavefunctions, conserved quantities and symmetries, and the harmonic oscillator. This guide says what each page teaches, the order to read them in, and the chapter's key equations.

blocks.text: The Foundations and Qubits chapters describe quantum states at one moment: what a state is, how to measure it, how a gate changes it. This chapter is about how states change by themselves, continuously, when a system is left alone with its energy. The rule is one equation, the Schrödinger equation, and the object that drives everything is the Hamiltonian $H$, the energy observable.

For quantum reservoir computing this is the central chapter. A quantum reservoir is a system that is left to evolve under a fixed Hamiltonian between inputs. How quickly it spreads an input across its qubits, which frequencies its features oscillate at, what it can never forget and what it can never see: every one of these is a question about $H$ and the evolution $e^{-iHt}$ it produces. By the end of the chapter you will be able to answer such questions for small systems by hand and for larger ones with a few lines of code.
Read the pages in this order

items: The Schrödinger Equation (#/quantum/dynamics/schrodinger-equation): the equation $\tfrac{d}{dt}\vert\psi\rangle = -iH\vert\psi\rangle$ and its solution $\vert\psi(t)\rangle = e^{-iHt}\vert\psi(0)\rangle$; why energy eigenstates only turn their phase; how to evolve any state by expanding it in eigenstates; a spin precessing in a magnetic field, a first look at Rabi oscillations, the energy-time speed limit, and solving the equation numerically.

Schrödinger and Heisenberg Pictures (#/quantum/dynamics/pictures-of-time-evolution): the same physics seen three ways. In the Schrödinger picture states move; in the Heisenberg picture observables move by $\tfrac{d}{dt}A = i[H, A]$; the interaction picture splits the motion into an easy part and a hard part, and gives the rotating frame used for every driven qubit. The page ends by reading the QRC feature formula in both pictures.

Wavefunctions, Position and Momentum (#/quantum/dynamics/wavefunctions): a particle that can be anywhere on a line, described by a wavefunction $\psi(x)$; momentum and the de Broglie relation; why $[x, p] = i\hbar$ gives the position-momentum uncertainty principle; the particle in a box as the worked example; and how a grid turns it back into matrices. This is the quantum mechanics of most textbooks; the page is background, since the QRC shelf works with qubits and oscillator modes rather than wavefunctions in space.

Symmetries and Conservation (#/quantum/dynamics/symmetries-and-conservation): how one commutator, $[H, A] = 0$, tells you a quantity is conserved forever; total-$Z$ and parity symmetry in spin models; splitting a Hamiltonian into blocks; why symmetries force degenerate energies; and what conserved quantities do to a reservoir.

The Harmonic Oscillator (#/quantum/dynamics/harmonic-oscillator): infinitely many evenly spaced levels derived from $[a, a^\dagger] = 1$; number states, coherent states and the Poisson statistics of photons; simulating an oscillator by truncation. The language of continuous-variable reservoirs.

blocks.text: Each page assumes the ones before it, and all of them assume the Foundations chapter (Foundations (#/quantum/foundations)) and the Bloch sphere and Pauli operators from Qubits (#/quantum/qubits). Two pages look ahead: the symmetries page writes two- and three-qubit states such as $\vert01\rangle$ and operators such as $X_1X_2$, explained on Composite Systems and Tensor Products (#/quantum/many-body/composite-systems), and the last section of the pictures page uses density matrices from Mixed States (#/quantum/many-body/mixed-states). Budget roughly an hour to an hour and a half per page if you work the check-yourself questions and problems, which is where the learning happens.
The key equations of the chapter

blocks.caption: The Schrödinger equation (ħ = 1) and its solution for a time-independent H. The state is rotated by the unitary U(t) = e^{−iHt}.

blocks.text: What it means: the Hamiltonian is the generator of time evolution. Knowing $H$ and the state now, you know the state at every later time; nothing is random until you measure.

blocks.caption: Expand in energy eigenstates; each coefficient just turns its phase at its own frequency E_k.

blocks.text: What it means: in the eigenbasis of $H$ nothing happens except phases turning. All the visible motion of averages comes from the differences $E_j - E_k$, which are the frequencies a reservoir's features oscillate at.

blocks.caption: How fast an average changes. If [H, A] = 0, A is conserved.

blocks.text: What it means: you can find conserved quantities without solving anything, just by checking commutators. A conserved quantity freezes a whole probability distribution and splits the state space into sectors.

blocks.caption: The harmonic oscillator: one commutator gives an evenly spaced ladder of energies.

blocks.text: What it means: an oscillator's energy comes in quanta of $\hbar\omega$ (photons, for light), and even its ground state has energy $\hbar\omega/2$.
One thing to keep in mind

Time evolution in this chapter is always unitary, so it never forgets anything: the overlap between two states, and so the distance between them, is preserved exactly. That is good for a quantum computer and bad for a reservoir, which must forget its distant past. The QRC shelf's whole treatment of fading memory starts from adding something non-unitary to these dynamics: measurement, resets or dissipation (The Echo State Property (#/qrc/foundations/echo-state-property) and Lindblad Dynamics (#/qrc/open-systems/lindblad-dynamics)). Learn the unitary case well first; it is the skeleton those pages build on.

After this chapter, Many Qubits (#/quantum/many-body) puts several qubits together: tensor products, entanglement, mixed states and the spin models that quantum reservoirs are made of. The interactive spin-model widgets there use the evolution $e^{-iHt}$ you learn here.
